'''''Averrhoa carambola''''' is a species of tree in the family [[Oxalidaceae]] native to tropical [[Southeast Asia]];<ref name="Gepts"/> it has a number of common names, including '''carambola''', '''star fruit''' and '''five-corner'''.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=6158|title=Taxonomy - GRIN-Global Web v 1.10.3.6|website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov|access-date=2019-02-24}}</ref> It is a small tree or shrub that grows {{convert|5|to|12|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, with rose to red-purple flowers. The flowers are small and bell-shaped, with five petals that have whitish edges. The flowers are often produced year round under tropical conditions. The tree is cultivated in tropical and semitropical regions for [[Carambola|its edible fruits]].

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Leaves- both sides I IMG 8443.jpg|thumb|Leaves – both sides, in India]]
[[File:Averrhoa carambola flowers.jpg|thumb|Flowers]]
The species in the genus ''Averrhoa'' along with the species in genus ''[[Sarcotheca]]'' are the only woody, tree-like plants belonging to the Oxalis family Oxalidaceae. The Oxalis family has nearly 900 species; most are herbaceous perennials or annuals native from tropical and semitropical locations, although a number also grow in other parts of the world. ''Averrhoa'' has sometimes been placed in the family Averrhoaceae.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomygenus.aspx?id=1191|title=GRIN-Global Web v 1.10.3.6|website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov|access-date=2019-02-24}}</ref> ''Averrhoa carambola'' is one of two species in the genus ''Averrhoa'', both have edible fruit; the other species [[Averrhoa bilimbi|''A. bilimbi'']], which is sometimes called the bilimbi or the cucumber tree, is limited to tropical regions. The fruits of ''A. bilimbi'' are too sour to be eaten raw, while the sweet forms of ''A. carambola'' are eaten raw. The fruits of ''A. bilimbi'' and the sour forms—which have high [[oxalic acid]] content—of ''A. carambola'' are pickled and made into jelly, jam, and juice.{{cn|date=August 2024}}

The genus was named after Abū 'l-Walīd Muḥammad bin Aḥmad bin Rushd (better known just as Ibn Rushd), who was called [[Averroes]] in European literature -  a famous Arabian physician,<ref name=DeborahSaturday>{{citation | last1 = Deborah | first1 = Pauline | last2 = Waller | first2 = Ridling  | title = Glow with stars | url = http://www.hindu.com/mp/2006/02/04/stories/2006020400060700.htm | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090810025041/http://www.hindu.com/mp/2006/02/04/stories/2006020400060700.htm | url-status = dead | archive-date = 10 August 2009 | location=Chennai, India | journal = [[The Hindu]] | date=4 February 2006}}</ref> [[astronomer]] and [[philosopher]] of the 12th century.<ref name=Quattrocchi2000>{{Citation| last = Quattrocchi | first =  Umberto| year = 2000| title = CRC world dictionary of plant names : common names, scientific names, eponyms, synonyms, and etymology| pages = 241| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=A68qyOyhOdkC&q=Averrhoa+named+after&pg=PA241| isbn = 0-8493-2673-7| publisher = CRC Press| location = Boca Raton}}</ref>

Past synonyms include:<ref name=":2">[http://mansfeld.ipk-gatersleben.de/pls/htmldb_pgrc/f?p=185:46:3709627839625571::NO::module,mf_use,source,akzanz,rehm,akzname,taxid:mf,,botnam,0,,Averrhoa%20carambola,11132 "Averrhoa carambola L"] ipk-gatersleben.de.</ref>
* ''Averrhoa pentandra'' Blanco, Fl. Filip., 392. 1837.
* ''Averrhoa acutangula'' Stokes, Bot. Mat. Med. vol. 2, 543. 1812.
* ''Connaropsis philippica'' Villar in Blanco, Fl. Filip. ed. vol. 3, app. 33. 1880.
The tree and fruits have many different names, ''carambola'' is the Spanish [[vernacular name]] of the tree.<ref name=DeborahSaturday/> In English it is called star fruit, five-corner or carambola,<ref>{{cite book |last=House of Commons of the Parliament of Great Britain  |title=Parliamentary Papers, House of Commons and Command, Volume 54 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MmkTAAAAYAAJ&q=%22chinese+gooseberry%22+averrhoa&pg=PA203 |access-date=30 May 2013|year=1884 |page=203}}</ref> in Malaysia and the Philippines it has numerous names.<ref name=Quattrocchi2000/> In [[Indonesia]] it is called ''belimbing'', in Tagalog it is called ''balimbing''. The related [[Averrhoa bilimbi|bilimbi]] is called ''kamias'' in Tagalog. In French, the tree is called ''carambolier'' and the fruit ''carambole''.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" />

==Description==
[[File:Averrhoa carambola Blanco1.139-cropped.jpg|thumb|left|An illustration of the [[Carambola|fruit]], leaves, and flowers of ''Averrhoa carambola'']]
[[File:Carambola Seedling.jpg|thumb|Seedling]]
''Averrhoa carambola'' is a small, slow-growing evergreen tree with a short-trunk or a shrub. The branches are drooping and the [[wood]] is white and turns reddish.<ref name=Author1990>{{Citation|author=L.D. Kapoor| year = 1990| title = CRC handbook of ayurvedic medicinal plants| pages = 58| isbn = 0-8493-0559-4| publisher = CRC Press| location = Boca Raton, Fla.}}</ref> It has a bushy shape with many branches producing a broad, rounded crown. The compound leaves are soft, medium-green, they are spirally arranged around the branches in an alternate fashion. The pinnate leaves have a single terminal leaflet and 5 to 11 nearly opposite leaflets, each leaf is 15–20 cm long, and the 3.8–9 cm long leaflets are ovate or ovate-oblong in shape. The top sides of the leaves are smooth and the undersides are finely hairy and whitish. The leaflets are reactive to light and tend to fold together at night, they are also sensitive to abrupt shock and when shaken tend to close up also. The lilac or purple-streaked, downy, flowers are produced in the axils of leaves at the end of twigs. The flowers are arranged in small clusters on the ends of the branches or sometimes on the larger stems and trunk, each cluster is attached to the tree with red stalks.  The bell-shaped, perfect flowers, are produced in loose panicles that are much-branched with pedicellate flowers; each flower is around 6 mm wide, with five petals that have recurved ends.  The fruits are showy with an oblong shape: they are longitudinally five to six-angled and 6.35–15 cm long and up to 9 cm wide. The fruits have a thin, waxy skin that is orange-yellow colored. The juicy fruits are yellow inside when ripe and have a crisp texture and when cut in cross-section are star-shaped. The fruits have an oxalic acid odor, which varies between plants from strong to mild, the taste also varies from very sour to mildly sweetish.  Each fruit may have up to twelve 6–12.5 mm long seeds, which are flat, thin and brown. Some cultivated forms produce fruits with no seeds.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ntbg.org/plants/plant_details.php?plantid=1377 |title=Averrhoa carambola - Meet the Plants - National Tropical Botanical Garden Plant Database |access-date=2008-12-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120526062957/http://ntbg.org/plants/plant_details.php?plantid=1377 |archive-date=2012-05-26 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=Editors2002>{{Citation|editor=P.K. Warrier|others=Illustrations by R. Vasudevan Nair| year = 2002| title = Indian medicinal plants : a compendium of 500 species| pages = 224| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=GkBRXzpqD98C&q=Averrhoa+carambola+description&pg=PA224| isbn = 81-250-0301-0| publisher = Orient Longman| location = Madras}}</ref>

=== Rapid plant movement ===
[[Rapid plant movement]] is seen in many plants and there are different mechanisms based on the speed of the movement and the situation the plant is in. Some plants may make movements within 2 seconds while some may take 20 seconds to complete a motion. Additionally, for some plants the movement can involve action potentials being activated,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Sukhov|first1=Vladimir|last2=Nerush|first2=Vladimir|last3=Orlova|first3=Lyubov|last4=Vodeneev|first4=Vladimir|date=2011-12-21|title=Simulation of action potential propagation in plants|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022519311004759|journal=Journal of Theoretical Biology|language=en|volume=291|pages=47–55|doi=10.1016/j.jtbi.2011.09.019|pmid=21959317|bibcode=2011JThBi.291...47S |issn=0022-5193|url-access=subscription}}</ref> or it can involve changes in water pressure and fluctuation of ions moving in and out of cells. In the case of the ''Averrhoa carambola'' plant it takes about 20 seconds for the leaves to move from their horizontal position to vertical. This mechanism involves the flux of ions and water. When the leaves receive an external stimulus (hands, herbivores) this will translate to an electrical stimulus which then leads to the flow of ions (specifically the potassium and chloride) out of the pulvinus. Within the pulvinus, there are flexor and extensor cells, and this is where the change of potassium and chloride concentration occurs. So as you can see in the diagram [where is the diagram?], when the cell is in its turgid state, the leaves are horizontal, and cells are filled with water. So when the chloride and potassium move out of the cells, the water will flux out which results in the leaves facing vertically. This movement of the leaves drooping takes only a couple of seconds as we saw in the video.<sup>{which video?]</sup> However, when the leaves or the tree is shaken, this will activate contractile proteins that are in the pulvinus, and they will cause the leaves to droop.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Marler|first1=Thomas E.|last2=Schaffer|first2=Bruce|last3=Crane|first3=Jonathan H.|date=1994-07-01|title=Developmental Light Level Affects Growth, Morphology, and Leaf Physiology of Young Carambola Trees|url=https://journals.ashs.org/view/journals/jashs/119/4/article-p711.xml|journal=Journal of the American Society for Horticultural Science|language=en-US|volume=119|issue=4|pages=711–718|doi=10.21273/JASHS.119.4.711|issn=2327-9788|doi-access=free}}</ref>

There are a few benefits of the drooping of the leaves: one is that it has been hypothesized that when the leaves droop it makes the plant look malnourished and unappealing, so herbivores are compelled to eat a different plant. Additionally, the movement helps the plant with reducing water loss<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Al-Yahyai|first1=Rashid|last2=Schaffer|first2=Bruce|last3=Davies|first3=Frederick S.|date=2005-12-01|title=Physiological Responses of Carambola Trees to Soil Water Depletion|url=https://journals.ashs.org/view/journals/hortsci/40/7/article-p2145.xml|journal=HortScience|language=en-US|volume=40|issue=7|pages=2145–2150|doi=10.21273/HORTSCI.40.7.2145|issn=0018-5345|doi-access=free}}</ref> as well as avoid damages.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Marler|first1=Thomas E.|last2=Lawton|first2=Patrick D.|date=1995-03-01|title=Movement Influences Carambola Leaflet Chlorophyll Fluorescence and Temperature under Sunny Conditions|url=https://journals.ashs.org/view/journals/jashs/120/2/article-p360.xml|journal=Journal of the American Society for Horticultural Science|language=en-US|volume=120|issue=2|pages=360–361|doi=10.21273/JASHS.120.2.360|issn=2327-9788|doi-access=free}}</ref>

The mechanism and reasoning for how this movement reduces water loss for plants is not fully known. However, one known mechanism is the closing of the stomatal pores which are the mouths of the plant in which gas exchange occurs. It takes in carbon dioxide which is important for photosynthesis. This movement of the stomatal pores is done by the guard cells that surround the pores. When there is not enough water in the air, the guard cells well release K+ ions into surrounding cells, and this causes water to move out of the guard cells.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=B. A.|first1=Biology|last2=A. S.|first2=Nursing|title=What's the Function of Stomata in Plant Tissue?|url=https://www.thoughtco.com/plant-stomata-function-4126012|access-date=2020-06-06|website=ThoughtCo|language=en}}</ref> After the water is moved out the guard cells shrink in size as well as the stomata pores, and this prevents water from escaping through the pores. This information was obtained through Yahyai's research on the starfruit tree's response to differing soil water depletion levels. Trees were grown in a greenhouse, and there were four levels of soil water depletion. Stomatal response, {{CO2}} levels, and transpiration were recorded and then analyzed.{{cn|date=August 2024}}

Finally, the drooping movement in the star fruit trees helps with reducing leaf damage, protecting it from increased leaf temperature, as well as losing photochemical efficiency (light energy being converted to be used for photosynthesis) from the sun. Excess radiation will act as a stimulus to these leaves, and they will respond with rapid movement. The leaf moving to a position that makes it parallel to the light source is important because the leaves will not be directly facing the sun. This information was found through recording sun to leaf area exposure, canopy diameter, and root growth. Trees had different levels of sun exposure, and how the tree responded was measured and analyzed.<ref name=":4" />[[File:Averrhoa carambola Fruit.JPG|thumb|Fruit]]

==Uses==
''Averrhoa carambola'' is best known as the star fruit, as it is best known for the star-like shape it has when cut. In addition to being eaten, the fruit is used in traditional Asian medicine to treat [[chickenpox]], [[intestinal parasite]]s, headaches, and other illnesses. Star fruit contains [[oxalate]], too much of which can be dangerous.

Starfruit juice can be used to remove stains from linen.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Hargreaves|first1=Dorothy|last2=Hargreaves|first2=Bob|title=Tropical Trees of the Pacific|year=1970|publisher=Hargreaves|location=Kailua, Hawaii|page=56}}</ref>

===Cultivation===
[[File:Fruits, leaves & Trunk I IMG 8445.jpg|thumb|left|upright|Fruits, leaves and trunk]]
''Averrhoa carambola'' has a number of different forms differing in fruit taste, texture, and shape, some are very acidic and others are sweet. The plant is grown in Malaysia and Taiwan, with smaller concentrations in Thailand, Israel, The United States, Brazil, Philippines, China, Australia, Indonesia and the warmer parts of India and other areas of the world with the same climate. It has become a commercial crop in many of these locations, grown for its edible fruits.<ref name=Ray2002>{{Citation| last = Ray | first =  P.K.| year = 2002| title = Breeding tropical and subtropical fruits| pages = 307–09| url = https://books.google.com/books?id=zKQPyovGnM4C&q=Averrhoa+carambola+description&pg=PA307| isbn = 3-540-42855-0| publisher = Narosa Pub. Pub. House| location = New Delhi}}</ref> The flowers need cross-pollination to produce fruit, thus seed raised plants are variable. Plants may flower and bear fruit in about a year after seed [[germination]]. Larger plants may bloom year-round in tropical areas as long as environmental conditions are suitable, plants may have flowers, unripe and ripe fruit at the same time. Under other climate and environmental conditions, plants tend to bloom in spring, and then off and on again during the rest of the year. Many different cultivars are grown, most are selected to optimize fruit flavor and maximum fruit production for specific growing areas, with each country or region having their own specific selections.<ref name=Ray2002/>
[[File:Averrhoa carambola, Hong Kong Park, December 2019 01.jpg|thumb|''Averrhoa carambola'' shrub]]

==Toxicology==
Like several other plants of the family [[Oxalidaceae]], its fruits are rich in [[oxalic acid]], which is toxic in high concentrations.{{cn|date=August 2024}}

There have been reports of intoxication in dialysis and uremic patients caused by a [[neurotoxin]] called [[caramboxin]]<ref>{{cite journal|author=Garcia-Cairasco, N., Moyses-Neto, M., Del Vecchio, F., Oliveira, J. A. C., dos Santos, F. L., Castro, O. W., Arisi, G. M., Dantas, M., Carolino, R. O. G., Coutinho-Netto, J., Dagostin, A. L. A., Rodrigues, M. C. A., Leão, R. M., Quintiliano, S. A. P., Silva, L. F., Gobbo-Neto, L. and Lopes, N. P.|date=2013|title= Elucidating the Neurotoxicity of the Star Fruit|journal=Angew. Chem. Int. Ed.|volume= 52|issue=49|pages= 13067–13070| doi=10.1002/anie.201305382|pmid=24281890}}</ref><ref name=Carolino2002>{{Citation| last = Carolino | first =  R. O. G| year = 2002| title = Atividade Biológica e Purificação Parcial da Neurotoxina da Fruta Averrhoa carambola L. (Oxalidaceae). | publisher = Departamento de Bioquímica da Faculdade de Medicina de Ribeirão Preto - USP | location = Ribeirão Preto, SP, Brazil}}</ref> present in the fruit. Such toxin is normally filtered by the kidneys, but patients in dialysis or suffering from kidney deficiencies may show severe symptoms, in a few cases fatal,<ref name=Chang2002>{{cite journal | last1 = Chang | first1 = J.M. | last2 = Hwang | first2 = S.J. | last3 = KUO |display-authors=et al | year = 2000 | title = Fatal outcome after ingestion of star fruit (Averrhoa carambola) in uremic patients | journal = Am J Kidney Dis | volume = 35 | issue = 2| pages = 189–193 | doi=10.1016/s0272-6386(00)70325-8| pmid = 10676715 }}</ref> after drinking the [[Juice|fruit juice]].
